answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a Cosmos DB (DocumentDB/MongoDB API) account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources under that account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." resource_group_name = "..." location = "..." offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB API connection string for Cosmos DB: mongodb://<username>@<accountName>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<accountName>@. Username is usually in the form <dbuser>@<accountName> and TLS (ssl=true) is required. Port 10255 (TLS) is used for Cosmos DB MongoDB API.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Primary billing model is provisioned throughput measured in Request Units per second (RU/s) or autoscale RU/s; there is also a serverless option for small workloads. Additionally, Azure offers vCore-based dedicated cluster (M-series) options for dedicated MongoDB-compatible clusters (vCore billing) for high-throughput/dedicated deployments and some advanced features like vector indexes — so expect RU/s by default and vCore tiers for dedicated clusters.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Common auth for the MongoDB API is SCRAM (username/password) using the Cosmos DB account keys as the user credential (user often formatted as <user>@<account>). Historically the MongoDB API uses the MongoDB authentication mechanisms (SCRAM-SHA-1/SCRAM-SHA-256). Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integration for the MongoDB API is limited/preview and not universally available; if Entra auth is supported you must obtain an AAD access token and present it via the driver’s SASL/OAUTHBEARER or a supported authMechanism — but the typical, broadly supported approach is to use SCRAM with the account key.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python, use pymongo). Do NOT use the azure-cosmos SDK for MongoDB API access — the MongoDB wire protocol is served and you should use MongoDB drivers. There is not a separate service-specific MongoDB client SDK beyond the standard drivers.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Newer/documentdb clusters support vector index algorithms such as IVF, HNSW and DiskANN (depending on compute tier). Typical index creation is done with the MongoDB-style createIndex API on the collection specifying a vector index on the embedding field. Example (pseudo-command): db.products.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_ivf', vectorIndexType: 'ivf', vectorIndexConfig: { dimension: 512, nlist: 1024 } }) — exact option names may differ on the service; the pattern is a createIndex call with a 'vector' field type and index options specifying algorithm and dimension.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) does not expose the same built-in full-text/hybrid search as a dedicated search service; for full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search you typically integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) or another external search engine. MongoDB Atlas Search is not part of Cosmos DB; to get hybrid text+vector capabilities you would either push data to Azure Cognitive Search or use an external search engine that supports hybrid queries.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported wire protocol/version depends on the account SKU but modern deployments support up to recent MongoDB server wire versions (clusters can advertise MongoDB 6.x/7.0 compatibility in newer offerings). Many administrative and server-side features of a native MongoDB server are not available: you do not have full admin/server access, you cannot install server-side modules, filesystem-level access is not available, and some niche commands and lower-level replication/backup admin commands are restricted. Some aggregation operators or latest server-only features may be missing or behave slightly differently — test against the target account version.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator that reproduces the MongoDB API behavior of Azure Cosmos DB; for local development run a local MongoDB server compatible with the target wire version (for example docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:7.0) and connect on port 27017. The official Azure Cosmos DB Emulator historically does not support the MongoDB API feature set, so using a matching local mongod image is the practical approach.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported on MongoDB API accounts that advertise a compatible server version (they require an oplog-like capability). On Cosmos DB’s MongoDB API change stream support exists for modern versions, and you generally do not need extra toggles beyond using a cluster/account that supports change streams — but older or lower-tier accounts might not have it. Verify support on the target account before relying on it.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The dedicated MCP server for this service is the 'documentdb' MCP server (the repo/agent profile named documentdb in the environment). The general Azure MCP server does not automatically provide documentdb-specific data-plane inspection tools; use the documentdb MCP server’s tooling/profile (default connection profile) to inspect Cosmos DB/MongoDB API collections, indexes and query plans.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft’s hosted DocumentDB service was the precursor name; that platform evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. 'DocumentDB' was the original name for the Azure proprietary document database that became Cosmos DB (SQL API). Azure Cosmos DB now supports multiple APIs, including the MongoDB-compatible API. Microsoft’s old 'DocumentDB' is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB — Cosmos DB is a proprietary, multi-model managed service that emulates several query/driver APIs (including MongoDB).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Cosmos DB’s proprietary storage and query engine which implements the MongoDB wire protocol for the MongoDB API. That means application code uses standard MongoDB drivers and most MongoDB operations, but some server behaviours, admin commands, and edge-case features may differ. Expect to use MongoDB drivers unchanged for normal CRUD/aggregation operations, but test advanced features and admin operations against the service because behavior can diverge from a native MongoDB server.

answers.question: What database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name 'sample_retail_11' for all collections and operations.

answers.question: How should the sample store 512-dimension float embeddings as BSON binary with subtype 0x09 from Python?
answers.answer: Encode the float32 vector to little-endian bytes and wrap with bson.Binary with subtype 0x09. Example code: bson.Binary(np.array(vec, dtype=np.float32).tobytes(), subtype=0x09).

answers.question: What createIndex call will the sample use to request an IVF vector index for the embedding field?
answers.answer: Use a MongoDB-style createIndex on the embedding field with vector index options. Example (pseudo-code): db.products.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_ivf', vectorIndexType: 'ivf', vectorIndexConfig: { dimension: 512, nlist: 1024 } } ). The sample will call collection.create_index(...) with equivalent options via PyMongo.

answers.question: Which image-embedding model will the sample use to get 512-dimensional vectors?
answers.answer: Use a CLIP model that produces 512-d vectors, e.g. Hugging Face 'openai/clip-vit-base-patch32' via transformers: from transformers import CLIPProcessor, CLIPModel; processor = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32'); model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained('openai/clip-vit-base-patch32') — produce a normalized 512-d float32 embedding.

answers.question: How will the sample issue the vector search query to get top-8 nearest neighbors after encoding a query image?
answers.answer: The sample will rely on the server-side vector search facility exposed through the MongoDB API. It will present the query vector as BSON binary subtype 0x09 and call the collection's vector search operator (example pseudo-call): collection.find({ '$vectorSearch': { 'field': 'embedding', 'vector': <Binary>, 'k': 8, 'algorithm': 'ivf' } }) or use the corresponding aggregate stage if required. If exact syntax differs, fall back to client-side similarity on a small sample or use the server-side index inspection tools via the 'documentdb' MCP to determine the precise operator names before finalizing.
